html:
The Enxet are an Indigenous people of about 17,000 in the Gran Chaco of western Paraguay. They speak a language of the Enlhet-Enenlhet family, close to that of the Enlhet, and were once called Lengua by outsiders.

They were hunters and gatherers who also fished and kept small gardens. After the Paraguayan War ended in 1870, the state sold huge tracts of the Chaco to foreign buyers, and cattle ranches took Enxet land. Anglican missionaries arrived from 1888. Many Enxet became labourers on the ranches that now held their country.

In 2005 and 2006 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled that Paraguay had violated the rights of two Enxet communities by denying them their land. Their Chaco neighbours include the Nivaclé.
